nodes.t: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark
nodes.n: The origin point for the modern validity critique: general-capability benchmarks are treated as if they measure general ability, when their task construction cannot support that claim.

nodes.t: Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research
nodes.n: Pre-AI political science. It supplies the four-level concept→measurement ladder that the GenAI measurement framework runs on, which is why it sits at the root of this cluster.

nodes.t: Position: Evaluating Generative AI Systems Is a Social Science Measurement Challenge
nodes.a: Wallach, Desai, Cooper, Wang, Atalla, Barocas, Blodgett, Chouldechova, Vaughan, Jacobs, et al.
nodes.n: The hinge of your whole map. Argues ML jumps straight from a vague concept to an instrument with no systematisation step. Authored largely by the same MSR group that produces the reliance studies in the human cluster.

nodes.t: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
nodes.a: Bean, Kearns, Romanou, Hafner, Mayne, Batzner, Foroutan, et al.
nodes.n: 29 reviewers, 445 benchmarks. The empirical backbone of the validity critique — only a small minority of benchmarks used any uncertainty estimate, and roughly a quarter relied on convenience sampling.

nodes.t: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
nodes.a: Lambert, Pyatkin, Morrison, Miranda, Lin, Chandu, Dziri, Kumar, Zick, Choi, Smith, Hajishirzi
nodes.n: Turns the reward model itself into an object of evaluation. This is the literal join between your evaluation interest and your RL interest.

nodes.t: RM-Bench: Benchmarking Reward Models of Language Models with Subtlety and Style
nodes.a: Liu, Yao, Min, Cao, Hou, Li
nodes.n: Sharpens RewardBench by separating substance from style — a reward model that rewards verbosity scores well on the wrong axis.

nodes.t: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods
nodes.n: An early benchmark built adversarially against a known failure mode rather than sampled from convenience. Frequently the gold-standard reference in reward-hacking papers.

nodes.t: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
nodes.a: Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov, Carter
nodes.n: Names the programme: features as the unit, circuits as the composition, and the polysemanticity problem that everything downstream tries to dissolve.

nodes.t: Toy Models of Superposition
nodes.n: The most load-bearing node in this cluster. Formalises superposition and lays out the three strategies for recovering features — strategy two is what became the SAE literature.

nodes.t: Taking Features Out of Superposition with Sparse Autoencoders
nodes.n: Circulated as an interim report rather than a paper, but repeatedly cited as the first application of SAEs to superposition. A good example of a node a keyword search would miss and a citation graph catches.

nodes.t: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
nodes.n: The demonstration that made SAEs the default tool: a one-layer transformer decomposed into interpretable features, with expansion factors up to 256×.

nodes.t: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
nodes.n: The parallel result to Bricken et al., and the one that ties SAE features back to a known circuit by localising the indirect-object-identification behaviour more finely than prior decompositions.

nodes.t: Interpretability in the Wild: A Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 Small
nodes.n: The reference circuit. Its value to the field is as a ground truth that later methods get checked against.

nodes.t: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
nodes.a: Templeton, Conerly, Marcus, Batson, et al.
nodes.n: Same method as Towards Monosemanticity at production scale, which is what moved SAEs from demonstration to tooling.

nodes.t: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders
nodes.a: Gao, la Tour, Tillman, et al.
nodes.n: Note the title's second verb. Introduces k-sparse autoencoders and, more importantly for you, treats SAE quality as a measurement problem rather than a demo.

nodes.t: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
nodes.a: Rajamanoharan, Conmy, Smith, Lieberum, Varma, Kramár, Shah, Nanda
nodes.n: Architectural fix for the shrinkage that L1 sparsity penalties impose on feature magnitudes.

nodes.t: Towards a Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
nodes.n: Sits in this cluster but is cited constantly from the human cluster. Its claim — that interpretability claims need human-subject validation — is exactly the seam between your interpretability and human-centred interests.

nodes.t: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
nodes.n: Finds that pushing the MSE–L0 Pareto frontier does not necessarily buy monosemanticity. Thematically this is a construct-validity argument aimed at interpretability, though it cites the interpretability canon rather than the measurement one.

nodes.t: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
nodes.a: Ouyang, Wu, Jiang, Almeida, Wainwright, Mishkin, et al.
nodes.n: InstructGPT. Establishes the RLHF pipeline whose failure modes the rest of this cluster studies, and serves as the synthetic gold reward model in the overoptimization work.

nodes.t: Specification Gaming: The Flip Side of AI Ingenuity
nodes.a: Krakovna, Uesato, Mikulik, Rahtz, Everitt, Kumar, et al.
nodes.n: The catalogue of agents satisfying the letter of an objective. Pre-LLM, and the conceptual ancestor of reward hacking.

nodes.t: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
nodes.n: Finds phase transitions — capability increases can flip a proxy from roughly aligned to actively harmful discontinuously, which is why monitoring a proxy score is not enough.

nodes.t: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
nodes.n: The quantitative statement of Goodhart's law for RLHF: proxy-versus-gold reward divergence grows with optimisation pressure in a predictable functional form. The most cited node in this cluster.

nodes.t: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
nodes.a: Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell, Ermon, Manning, Finn
nodes.n: Removes the explicit reward model, which was widely read as removing the reward-hacking surface. The next two nodes are the correction to that reading.

nodes.t: Disentangling Length from Quality in Direct Preference Optimization
nodes.n: DPO-trained models get longer throughout training without getting better past a point. Length is the cleanest observable instance of a proxy being gamed.

nodes.t: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms
nodes.a: Rafailov, Chittepu, Park, Sikchi, Hejna, Knox, Finn, Niekum
nodes.n: Shows direct alignment methods degrade the same way despite having no learned reward model, often before a single epoch completes. Overoptimization survives the removal of the thing it was blamed on.

nodes.t: SAFER: Probing Safety in Reward Models with Sparse Autoencoders
nodes.n: Points SAEs at reward models. This is the single most direct bridge on your map between mechanistic interpretability and the RL/evaluation question — it cites the interpretability canon wholesale while working on an alignment-training object.

nodes.t: Information-Theoretic Reward Modeling for Stable RLHF: Detecting and Mitigating Reward Hacking
nodes.n: A four-way bridge, and the reason it earns a place in a seed map: it cites the overoptimization line, both reward-model benchmarks, and a capability benchmark together. An information-bottleneck reward model plus a hacking indicator.

nodes.t: A Review of User Interface Design for Interactive Machine Learning
nodes.n: The pre-LLM interaction-design substrate. Still the reference for what an ML interface owes its user structurally.

nodes.t: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
nodes.a: Amershi, Weld, Vorvoreanu, Fourney, Nushi, Collisson, Suh, Iqbal, Bennett, Inkpen, Teevan, Kikin-Gil, Horvitz
nodes.n: 18 guidelines synthesised from two decades of work, validated with 49 practitioners against 20 shipped products. The hub of the human-centred design cluster and the thing later HCAI standards work orbits.

nodes.t: A Multidisciplinary Survey and Framework for Design and Evaluation of Explainable AI Systems
nodes.n: Organises XAI by who the explanation is for. Cites the design guidelines and the interpretability-rigour argument in the same breath, which makes it a structural connector.

nodes.t: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-Assisted Decision-Making
nodes.n: The most cited node in this cluster. Interventions that force deliberation cut overreliance — and are liked less by the people they help, which is the design tension the cluster keeps circling.

nodes.t: Building Machines that Learn and Think with People
nodes.a: Collins, Bhatt, Liu, Piriyakulkij, Sucholutsky, Ganguli, Lake, Weller, et al.
nodes.n: Frames models as thought partners rather than oracles or tools. The theoretical framing that recent overreliance work builds its motivation on.

nodes.t: To Rely or Not to Rely? Evaluating Interventions for Appropriate Reliance on Large Language Models
nodes.n: Tests reliance interventions head to head. Insists on appropriate reliance as the target — underreliance is a failure too, which most overreliance framings quietly ignore.

nodes.t: Fostering Appropriate Reliance on Large Language Models: The Role of Explanations, Sources, and Inconsistencies
nodes.n: Users read inconsistency as an unreliability cue and use sources to verify. Note the author list — Vaughan and Liao also sit on the measurement-theory work in the evaluation cluster.

nodes.t: Contrastive Explanations That Anticipate Human Misconceptions Can Improve Human Decision-Making Skills
nodes.n: Explanations aimed at the user's likely misconception rather than at the model's reasoning. Doshi-Velez appearing here is the interpretability/HCI seam in author form.

nodes.t: Measuring and Mitigating Overreliance to Build Human-Compatible AI
nodes.n: Argues the conversational, open-ended nature of LLMs breaks the measurement instruments overreliance research inherited from AI-assisted decision-making. A measurement-validity argument raised inside the human cluster.

nodes.t: Behavioral Indicators of Overreliance During Interaction with Conversational Language Models
nodes.a: Liu, Zhou, Shen, Liu, Wu, Chen
nodes.n: 77 participants, an LLM seeded with plausible misinformation, three realistic tasks. Derives behavioural signatures of overreliance from interaction logs — whole-paragraph copy-paste, skipped comprehension, coarse navigation.

nodes.t: From Trust to Appropriate Reliance: Measurement Constructs in Human-AI Decision-Making
nodes.n: A systematic review asking whether the field's reliance constructs are coherent. Structurally the best entry point on the map: it reaches back to the 2017–2021 foundations and forward into the current CHI work.

nodes.t: Validating and Refining Measurements for Generative AI Evaluation via Stakeholder Engagement
nodes.a: Nguyen, Garcia-Gathright, Washington, Chouldechova, Wallach, Vaughan
nodes.n: Takes the measurement framework and asks the people affected whether the instrument measures the right thing. This is where human-centred method and evaluation methodology stop being separate interests.

nodes.t: Survey on joint compression and fine-tuning of large language models: Methods, toolchains, and open challenges under resource constraints
nodes.a: Jihyeon Kim, Hanyong Lee, Jaesung Lee
nodes.n: Surveys methods for jointly compressing and fine-tuning LLMs under resource constraints, citing lin2021 (quantization) and ouyang2022 (RLHF-based instruction tuning) as foundational techniques. It maps the toolchain landscape rather than proposing new results, situating RLHF-style fine-tuning alongside compression as a resource-efficiency challenge.

nodes.t: Leveraging Low-Level Symbolic Competences for Unsupervised Grounding in Hallucination Detection
nodes.n: Proposes a neurosymbolic hallucination detection pipeline that has an LLM build a SQL database from reference documents and checks responses against it for grounding, evaluated on RAGTruth and DiaHalu. It targets a core evaluation methodology problem (detecting unsupported LLM outputs) using a low-level symbolic competence as an unsupervised signal, distinct from the RLHF alignment framing of ouyang2022.

nodes.t: IDEEA: training-free Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching
nodes.a: Zheng Wang, Muchen Li, Renjie Liao, Yan Leng
nodes.n: Introduces IDEEA, a training-free activation-steering method that computes input-specific steering directions via per-head clustering and optimal matching, rather than a single fixed direction shared across inputs. It advances mechanistic control of LLM internals as a cheaper alternative to weight-update alignment methods like the RLHF fine-tuning used in ouyang2022.

nodes.t: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
nodes.a: Minglai Yang, Xinyu Guo, Mihai Surdeanu, Liangming Pan
nodes.n: Introduces sparse autoencoders trained to align learned features with predefined concepts, building on prior SAE feature-analysis work. This pushes interpretability research toward more controllable, human-labeled concept spaces rather than purely unsupervised feature discovery.

nodes.t: Navigating maritime emergencies with large models: A lifecycle-oriented review
nodes.a: Jing Xu, Qingqing Yang, Zhiwei Yang, Yingying Gao, Kewei Yang, Jiang Jiang
nodes.n: abstract too thin to summarise

nodes.t: From Curiosity to Caution: How Expertise Shapes the Use of Interpretable Machine Learning
nodes.a: Syeda Masooma Naqvi, Gayathri Balaji, Angelique Laju, Harmanpreet Kaur
nodes.v: Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency
nodes.n: An interview study (N=23) showing that novice and expert data scientists use interpretability tools differently, with novices driven by curiosity and experts by efficiency concerns. It extends work on socio-organizational factors in interpretability adoption, arguing tool design must account for user proficiency level rather than treating all users uniformly.

nodes.t: Hallucinations in Organization-backed AI advisors: Evidence about Skepticism, Verification, and Reliance in Goal-Directed Use
nodes.a: Simon J. Blanchard, Aaron M. Garvey, Laura O'Laughlin
nodes.n: abstract too thin to summarise

nodes.t: Justified or Just Convincing? Error Verifiability as a Dimension of LLM Quality
nodes.a: Xiaoyuan Zhu, K. Truong, Riccardo Fogliato, Gokul Swamy, Wei-Jia Zhang, Minglai Yang, Long Ye, Bang Liu, Ming-Hao Liu, Andrew Ilyas, Steven Z. Wu
nodes.n: Proposes 'error verifiability'—whether a user can actually tell when an LLM answer is wrong—as a quality dimension distinct from surface plausibility or confidence. Builds on overreliance and persuasiveness (bo2025) literatures to argue that convincing-but-unverifiable outputs drive miscalibrated trust in human-AI interaction.
